hero.lede: We develop the Triangular Spatial Relationship (TSR) method: an alignment-free way of representing a 3D protein structure as a set of integer keys, so that structures can be compared, clustered and searched without superimposition. This site documents the method, the TSR-derived methods built on it, and the public Python packages that implement them.

researchVision.heading: Toward Deciphering Molecular Recognition
researchVision.question: Is there a general molecular recognition code that governs how biomolecules recognize one another and how those interactions reshape molecular structure?
researchVision.intro: TSR transforms molecular 3D geometry into interpretable integer descriptors that can be compared across structures to identify conserved, altered, and interaction-associated spatial patterns.
researchVision.direction: Our long-term goal is to combine these interpretable structural descriptors with machine learning, AI-generated structures, and simulation-derived ensembles to connect structural prediction with mechanistic understanding.
researchVision.detailsLabel: Read more about our research vision
details: Biomolecular interactions can produce structural changes ranging from subtle local atomic rearrangements to larger conformational shifts. A continuing challenge is not only to generate or predict molecular structures, but also to determine which geometric features are conserved, altered, or specifically associated with recognition and binding.

TSR represents molecular 3D structures through triangular spatial relationships encoded as discrete integer keys. These descriptors make it possible to quantify structural relationships and investigate recurring or interaction-associated geometric signatures at global, local, and atomic scales. The TSR framework has been extended across proteins, amino acids, ligands, drugs, nucleotides, carbohydrates, and biomolecular interaction interfaces.

By combining TSR-based analysis with machine learning and structures generated through AI-guided prediction or physics-based simulation, we aim to identify structural determinants of molecular recognition and investigate whether common recognition principles emerge across different biomolecular systems.

introduction.heading: How TSR represents a structure
introduction.body: TSR takes the Cα atoms of a protein as the vertices of triangles. Every triangle is reduced to a single integer — its key — computed from the triangle's side lengths, its angles and the labels of its vertices. Identical triangles in different proteins receive the same key, so two structures can be compared by counting the keys they share, with no alignment step and no superimposition.

figure.alt: Six-step diagram of the TSR pipeline: an input 3D protein structure; its representative Cα coordinates selected; triangular motifs constructed between triplets of those points; the geometric features of a triangle measured as its maximum distance, angle bin and vertex labels; those features mapped deterministically to TSR keys; and the keys counted into a key-frequency vector used for structural similarity and machine learning. A footnote reads: no structural superposition required.
figure.caption: From a structure, to triangles between its Cα atoms, to one integer key per triangle, to a vector describing the whole protein.

methods.heading: TSR-based methods
methods.intro: The core representation has been extended in several directions — grouping amino acids, discriminating mirror images, comparing structures of different sizes, adding secondary structure, and moving beyond a single protein to drugs, ligands and nucleotides. Each method has its own page with installation instructions and a worked tutorial.

analysis.heading: Key analysis and visualisation
analysis.intro: Once keys have been generated, a second family of tools summarises and interprets them: finding the keys shared across a set of structures, clustering structures by key similarity, and training models on key frequencies.

software.heading: Software and source code
software.intro: Every method on this site is implemented in a public repository. The packages are installed from source with pip; the method pages carry the exact commands and the expected input formats.

group.heading: The research group
group.intro: TSR is developed jointly by the Department of Chemistry and the School of Computing and Informatics at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette, bringing together faculty, doctoral researchers and undergraduate students from chemistry, biology and computer science.

contact.heading: Working with us
contact.body: We welcome questions about the method, about using the packages on your own structures, and about research collaboration. Problems with the software are best reported as issues on the relevant repository.
